title: Wat Khao Nang Buat, Nakhon Nayok: 227-Step Hilltop Temple | ThailandAddict
metaDesc: A guide to Wat Khao Nang Buat in Nakhon Nayok, Thailand — a small hilltop temple where 227 steps lead to a century-old Buddha footprint and open views over the rice fields. With how to get there, opening hours, and nearby stops.

eyebrow: Things to do in Nakhon Nayok
h1:
Wat Khao Nang Buat
Climb to the shrine, take in the rice-field views
intro: Wat Khao Nang Buat is a temple sitting on a low hill in Sarika sub-district, Mueang Nakhon Nayok. The draw is the flight of 227 steps that climbs to the mondop at the top, where you'll find a Buddha footprint replica more than a hundred years old and wide-open views across the rice fields and the ridgelines around town. It's a merit-making spot where you get to pay respects and squeeze in a bit of exercise at the same time.

blocks.html: If you're visiting Nakhon Nayok around the Sarika Waterfall area and want a stop that isn't another waterfall or cafe, Wat Khao Nang Buat is worth a look. It's a small temple on a hill, and the thing people talk about is the 227 steps you have to climb to reach the mondop at the top. That sounds like a lot, but take it slow and rest in stages and you'll get there. Once you're up top, the view and the cool breeze make the effort worth it.

blocks.text: Climbing the 227 steps to the top

blocks.html: The temple's staircase is a long concrete one running up the hill, with handrails on both sides. The climb from the base to the top is around 100 metres of elevation — not steep like a real mountain, but enough to leave you a little out of breath if you don't exercise regularly. The trick is to walk slowly, pause at the seating spots along the way, and turn around to watch the view below open up wider with every step.

items: Start in the morning or late afternoon — midday sun is harsh and the steps get hot. Before 10am or after 3pm is much more comfortable.
Wear shoes you can walk in — some steps are uneven in height, so trainers or anything snug are easier than flip-flops.
Bring water up with you — there are no shops at the top, so carry a bottle along.

blocks.text: What there is to pay respects to at the top

blocks.html: Once you reach the top, the centrepiece is the mondop housing the Buddha footprint replica, which is over a hundred years old (made around 1858) and revered by locals. Inside the mondop there's also a blessing-pose Buddha image and several other old Buddha statues to pay respects to. If you're into merit-making, you get to pay respects and ask for blessings all in one spot.

blocks.title: What to know before you go
blocks.html: The temple is open roughly 08:00–16:00 daily, free with no admission fee. Just watch the time — if you arrive late in the afternoon you may not make it up and down before closing. Allow around 45 minutes to an hour for the climb up, down, and taking in the view.

blocks.text: Town and rice-field views from the top

blocks.html: What makes people willing to climb up is the view from the top — an open outlook over green rice fields alternating with the ridgelines around Nakhon Nayok town. The breeze is cool and pleasant up there since you're above the flatland. The prettiest stretch is the rainy season into early winter when the fields are still green, plus mornings or evenings when the sun is soft and the light photographs well. It's a photo spot that fewer people have found compared to the famous waterfalls.

items.name: Rice-field viewpoint
items.blurb: From the platform at the top you look out over paddy fields and houses below — at its best when the fields are green in the rainy season.

items.name: Ridgelines around town
items.blurb: The other side looks out over the hills ringing Nakhon Nayok, with long views on a clear day.

items.name: Buddha footprint mondop
items.blurb: The focal point at the top — both a place to pay respects and a backdrop for photos with the view.

blocks.html: The temple is in Sarika sub-district, Mueang district, about 10–15 minutes by car from Nakhon Nayok town and on the same route as the Sarika Waterfall zone. Driving yourself is easiest since there's a car park at the base of the hill. Coming from Bangkok it's around a 2-hour drive, and it makes a good stop on the way to the waterfalls or cafes around Sarika.

items: Sarika Waterfall — Nakhon Nayok's well-known waterfall, in the same zone, so you can stop by straight after.
Huai Prue Reservoir — a reservoir viewpoint near the temple with easy parking, good for mountain-view photos.
Cafes around Sarika — there are several hill-view cafes in this area, perfect for a rest after coming down.

blocks.title: Dress appropriately
blocks.html: This is a temple, so dress modestly — skip spaghetti straps or very short shorts so you can comfortably enter and pay respects in the mondop.

faq.q: How many steps do you have to climb at Wat Khao Nang Buat?
faq.a: The concrete staircase from the base to the mondop at the top has 227 steps in total, around 100 metres of elevation. It isn't very steep, but take it slowly and rest at the seating spots along the way.

faq.q: What time does Wat Khao Nang Buat open, and is there an admission fee?
faq.a: It's open roughly 08:00–16:00 daily, free with no admission fee. Allow around 45 minutes to an hour for the climb up and down and taking in the view, and don't arrive too late in the afternoon near closing time.

faq.q: What is there to pay respects to at the top of the hill?
faq.a: There's a mondop housing a Buddha footprint replica over a hundred years old, along with a blessing-pose Buddha image and several other old Buddha statues, plus views over the rice fields and the ridgelines around town.

faq.q: Is Wat Khao Nang Buat far from Nakhon Nayok town?
faq.a: It's in Sarika sub-district, Mueang district, about 10–15 minutes by car from town, on the same route as the Sarika Waterfall zone. Driving yourself is easiest since there's a car park at the base of the hill.

faq.q: When are the views from Wat Khao Nang Buat at their best?
faq.a: From the rainy season into early winter when the rice fields are still green, and in the morning or evening when the sun is soft and the light photographs well — the weather is also cooler for the climb.
